'Reindeer boy' is the nickname some people jokingly use for Erdene, a cheerful ten-year-old from a family of reindeer herders. Erdene lives in a remote region of north-western Mongolia that can only be reached by horseback or helicopter. Each morning, he wakes to the sound of water trickling over smooth river stones. He crawls out of his family's branch-framed tepee and walks down to the stream, cupping his hands to splash the cold, clear water over his face. The place feels like a quiet paradise - fitting, since Erdene's own name means 'treasure'.

Erdene's diet consists mostly of hunted meat, rice and flour. In winter, once the snow has frozen everything solid, his mother collects water by melting blocks of ice chopped from the frozen river.

The family's herd of reindeer grazes on wild mushrooms and the leaves of red and yellow shrubs and willow trees. The reindeer provide milk and cheese, and carry the herders deep into the forest to hunt. But the reindeer population is shrinking, and the surrounding wildlife is disappearing too. A family needs at least 100 reindeer to sustain their way of life; right now, families average only around 14. Many of these reindeer-herding families, known as the Tsaatan people, have given up and abandoned a lifestyle that stretches back for centuries.

Erdene doesn't dwell on his family's hardships. He helps out around the tepee - cleaning, chopping firewood, milking the reindeer. Once the snow melts, he loves riding a trotting reindeer, laughing as he tries to keep up with the herd.

Deep Cover

Mira watched through the open cargo door as the small twin-engine plane banked low over the dense canopy of the Amazon jungle. The tangled treetops rushed past beneath them like an endless green ocean, each leaf catching the last of the afternoon light. They were flying so low that Mira felt she could almost reach out and skim her fingers across the leaves. She fixed her eyes on the jungle below and thought to herself that whoever had designed this part of the world had clearly been showing off.

Without warning the plane dropped sideways as it hit a pocket of turbulence. Mira's shoulder slammed into the cold metal wall as the enormous man overseeing the mission launched into another furious rant at the pilot.

'Where'd you get your licence, out of a cereal box? My nephew could fly better than this, and he's six.'

Mira was almost impressed. She'd dealt with plenty of Vantage's men over the years, and 'licence' was the longest word she'd ever heard one of them use correctly.

The pilot's expression didn't change at all. He'd clearly been warned about this particular passenger and had stuffed his ears with cotton wool so the shouting couldn't reach him.

The well-dressed heavy beside him tightened his seatbelt and pulled out an embroidered handkerchief to mop his forehead. The smaller man next to him eyed it doubtfully.

'Embroidered?' he smirked.

'A gift from my daughter,' the first man snapped, in a tone that was clearly meant as a warning, his nerves showing more than usual.

He'd been on edge since take-off, and if Mira's instincts were right, the pilot was an expert and was thoroughly enjoying every bit of 'accidental' turbulence along the way.

Just then, the smaller man doubled over and filled another paper bag with the contents of his lunch. Mira caught the ghost of a smile crossing the pilot's face.

She adjusted the small parachute strapped to her back and crawled quietly across the floor of the cargo hold, past crates stacked like oversized dice. Taking out her multitool, she carefully worked the seal off one of the crates until she found it: a small metal case that, if she was right, held exactly what she'd been sent to find - and it was her job to get it before the plane landed and delivered it straight into Vantage's hands.

Living lights of the deep

Far below the ocean's surface, where sunlight never reaches, an eerie kind of light still glows in the darkness. This natural light, produced by living creatures, is called bioluminescence, and scientists estimate that as many as 90 per cent of deep-sea animals are able to produce it in some way.

Bioluminescence happens when a chemical inside an animal's body reacts with oxygen, producing light without producing much heat at all - unlike a lightbulb, which wastes most of its energy as heat instead of light. Different creatures use this glow for very different reasons. Some, like the anglerfish, dangle a glowing lure above their mouths to attract curious prey close enough to snap up. Others use bioluminescence purely for defence: certain species of squid release a glowing cloud of ink instead of a dark one, momentarily blinding a predator so the squid can escape unseen.

Perhaps the most surprising use of bioluminescence is for communication. Some species of deep-sea fish flash complex patterns of light to attract a mate, not unlike the way fireflies flicker to one another on a summer evening above ground. Scientists studying these light patterns have discovered that many species produce a light unique to them, almost like a signature, allowing individuals to recognise their own kind in the pitch-black water.

Not all bioluminescent creatures live in the deep sea, either. Certain kinds of plankton, tiny organisms drifting near the ocean's surface, glow brightly when disturbed by movement in the water. On some beaches at night, waves breaking on the shore can trigger a shimmering blue glow along the water's edge, an effect that has drawn curious visitors to certain coastlines for generations.

Despite decades of study, scientists believe there is still a great deal to learn about bioluminescence. New deep-sea expeditions continue to discover previously unknown glowing species living at depths humans have only recently been able to explore.

The tunnel twisted and dipped, opened briefly into a small hollow, then narrowed again into a gap that Priya could barely squeeze through. Beyond it lay another long, crooked passage that led back down, in a series of rough steps, to the cave they'd first entered. Tired, confused and more than a little disappointed, Priya stumbled out onto the hillside, her friends trailing behind her. Her torch flickered and died, leaving them shivering in the moonlit dark.

'Did it just loop back around?' asked Tess. 'Or did we take a wrong turn somewhere?'

'Should we go back through?' said Ben. 'Maybe we missed a turn.'

'I don't think we did,' Marcus said quietly. 'Look!'

They all turned and looked out over the valley.

The lake gleamed silver under the moon, its familiar dark islands scattered like lumps of coal. They could see the same snow-capped ridge and the same distant hills to the west, just as they'd seen them a thousand times before.

What was different was Fenwick House. There was no mismatched roofline, no tangled garden hedges. Where the crumbling ruin usually stood was a tall, grim stone tower, with narrow slit windows and a moat of dark water.

'We actually did it,' Priya breathed. 'I can't believe it.'

A sudden rush of excitement overtook the four friends, and they whooped and spun in circles, their packs banging against their backs. Just as suddenly, seriousness settled back over them. What had they actually done?

In that moment, all four realised they hadn't truly believed it was possible to travel back in time. The whole thing had felt like a game, something they'd pretended to believe while secretly knowing it was made up. Now, though, they understood it wasn't a game at all. They had left their own time behind and stepped into a world with entirely different rules. They could easily get hurt here, or trapped forever with no way home. It was a terrifying thought, one none of them wanted to face directly.

Through the gap

The tunnel twisted and dipped, opened briefly into a small hollow, then narrowed again into a gap that Priya could barely squeeze through. Beyond it lay another long, crooked passage that led back down, in a series of rough steps, to the cave they'd first entered. Tired, confused and more than a little disappointed, Priya stumbled out onto the hillside, her friends trailing behind her. Her torch flickered and died, leaving them shivering in the moonlit dark.

'Did it just loop back around?' asked Tess. 'Or did we take a wrong turn somewhere?'

'Should we go back through?' said Ben. 'Maybe we missed a turn.'

'I don't think we did,' Marcus said quietly. 'Look!'

They all turned and looked out over the valley.

The lake gleamed silver under the moon, its familiar dark islands scattered like lumps of coal. They could see the same snow-capped ridge and the same distant hills to the west, just as they'd seen them a thousand times before.

What was different was Fenwick House. There was no mismatched roofline, no tangled garden hedges. Where the crumbling ruin usually stood was a tall, grim stone tower, with narrow slit windows and a moat of dark water.

'We actually did it,' Priya breathed. 'I can't believe it.'

A sudden rush of excitement overtook the four friends, and they whooped and spun in circles, their packs banging against their backs. Just as suddenly, seriousness settled back over them. What had they actually done?

In that moment, all four realised they hadn't truly believed it was possible to travel back in time. The whole thing had felt like a game, something they'd pretended to believe while secretly knowing it was made up. Now, though, they understood it wasn't a game at all. They had left their own time behind and stepped into a world with entirely different rules. They could easily get hurt here, or trapped forever with no way home. It was a terrifying thought, one none of them wanted to face directly.
